liturgical_day: Tuesday of the Twenty-second Week in Ordinary Time
scripture_edition: Douay-AI, modernized from the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible.
title: His word was with power
theme: In the synagogue at Capharnaum, Christ's teaching and his command reveal one undivided authority. His word exposes evil, silences its false witness, frees the afflicted man, and leaves the assembly facing the power of the Holy One of God.
introduction: Luke follows the rejection at Nazareth with Jesus' descent to Capharnaum. He does not answer injury with withdrawal from his people. He teaches again on the sabbath, and the force of his word astonishes those who hear him. The Fathers gathered in the Catena Aurea dwell on the difference between Christ and every merely human teacher. He does not borrow authority or hide behind the formula of a messenger. The Master of the Law speaks in his own power, and his deeds make visible what his teaching declares. In the synagogue, an unclean spirit recognizes the threat posed by the Holy One of God. Yet Jesus accepts no testimony from a corrupt mouth and enters no negotiation with the oppressor. His brief command silences the spirit and releases the man. Even the final convulsion cannot overturn Christ's mercy: the man is thrown down, but not harmed. St Bede sees in that complete deliverance a sign meant to draw witnesses toward salvation, while St Ambrose places the whole scene within the renewal of creation. The sabbath, which marked the completion of the first creation, now becomes the setting in which the Son begins to restore what evil has disfigured. The assembly asks what kind of word can command unclean spirits with authority and power. Luke's answer is already standing before them: the word belongs to the Holy One, and what he commands he accomplishes.
hero_alt: Jesus commands an unclean spirit to leave a man in the synagogue at Capharnaum as the unharmed man falls and the assembly watches in astonishment, rendered in Byzantine mosaic, stained glass, gold leaf, and luminous geometry
closing: The people at Capharnaum do more than admire an eloquent teacher. They encounter a word that acts. Christ speaks, evil yields, and the person held under its power is restored without injury. That pattern asks something deeper from us than amazement. We often welcome the words of Jesus while reserving hidden rooms where fear, resentment, compulsion, or pride may continue to speak. The Gospel shows no rivalry between voices. The unclean spirit is noisy, but it is not sovereign. Jesus does not need spectacle or argument; his authority is sufficient. Bring before him whatever has made a home in you without belonging there. Do not mistake its persistence for ownership or its volume for power. At the same time, receive Christ's silence toward the demon as a lesson in discernment. Even a true title becomes corrupt when an unclean voice uses it to distract from obedience. The Lord asks us to know him through the word entrusted to the Church and through the freedom his grace produces. Let his command reach both thought and habit. The same Christ who taught openly in the synagogue still joins truth to healing. His word does not merely describe liberty from afar. It enters the place of bondage, breaks the claim of the oppressor, and restores the person whom evil tried to possess.

verses.text: Then he went down to Capharnaum, a city of Galilee, and taught them there on the sabbath days.
verses.author: St Ambrose of Milan
verses.insight: Jesus leaves Nazareth without carrying its hostility into his next encounter. Ambrose sees him remembering mercy rather than injury, continuing to soften unbelieving hearts by teaching and healing.
verses.commentary: Ambrose frames the descent to Capharnaum as an act of mercy after rejection. Neither indignation at Nazareth's treatment nor displeasure at its wickedness makes Jesus abandon Judea. He sets injuries aside and continues to seek the people, sometimes teaching and sometimes healing, so that hardened hearts may be softened. Cyril compares him to a good physician who visits even those suffering from a mortal disease, though he already knows their resistance. The verse therefore reveals the constancy of divine charity: human rejection does not turn Christ vindictive or idle; he goes on bringing the remedy.
verses.source_label: St Ambrose of Milan and St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:31–37

verses.text: And they were astonished at his teaching, for his word was with power.
verses.author: St Cyril of Alexandria
verses.insight: Christ speaks beyond the limits of a prophet because he is the Master of the Law. Cyril says his word does not merely soothe; it awakens hearers and presses them toward salvation.
verses.commentary: Cyril explains that the hearers perceive unusual might in Jesus' teaching. A prophet delivers a received message, but Christ does not need to preface his words with, “Thus says the Lord.” As Master of the Law, he carries its figures into their spiritual truth and speaks with an authority that belongs to him. His teaching is not empty severity, but a force that urges people to seek salvation. Bede adds a searching test for every teacher: speech has power when the speaker performs what he teaches. In Christ, word and life agree perfectly, so his doctrine bears the weight of his deeds.
verses.source_label: St Cyril of Alexandria and St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:31–37

verses.text: And in the synagogue there was a man who had an unclean devil, and he cried out with a loud voice,
verses.author: St Ambrose of Milan
verses.insight: The conflict surfaces in the very place of worship. Ambrose sees Christ's sabbath healing as the beginning of a renewed creation where the old order had reached its rest.
verses.commentary: Ambrose notices that the work of divine healing begins on the sabbath. The old creation had ended with sabbath rest; Christ now begins renewal at that point, showing that the Son is not trapped beneath the Law but is the Creator who completes his work. Cyril observes that Jesus joins mighty deeds to teaching because visible signs can awaken those whose reason has not yet risen to knowledge. The man's cry therefore interrupts nothing accidental. In the synagogue, Christ's authoritative teaching exposes the bondage hidden among the assembly, and the work of restoration begins where the word has brought evil into the open.
verses.source_label: St Ambrose of Milan and St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:31–37

verses.text: saying, ‘Let us alone! What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God.’
verses.author: St Athanasius of Alexandria
verses.insight: The title is true, but the witness is corrupt. Athanasius distinguishes Christ as the Holy One by nature, while warning that believers must not receive instruction from the devil.
verses.commentary: Athanasius attends closely to the title “the Holy One of God.” Christ is not one holy person among others; he is holy by nature, and all the saints are called holy by participation in him. Yet the demon's confession does not make the demon a trustworthy teacher. Cyril says such praise was a snare: the spirits hoped to stir vainglory and win relief from the one opposing them. The truth of a phrase cannot cleanse a corrupt intention. The verse teaches both Christology and discernment. We confess Jesus as the unique Holy One, but we learn that sacred words must not be detached from a holy source and obedient purpose.
verses.source_label: St Athanasius of Alexandria and St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:31–37

verses.text: Jesus rebuked him, saying, ‘Hold your peace and go out of him.’ And when the devil had thrown him into the midst, he went out of him and did not hurt him at all.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: Jesus permits the final convulsion to display the completeness of the cure. Bede stresses that the man is thrown down yet not harmed, so the Saviour's power is seen as restoration rather than destruction.
verses.commentary: Bede explains that God permits the man to be thrown into the midst so the Saviour's power may become evident and draw witnesses toward salvation. Luke's insistence that the man was not hurt clarifies the violence: the spirit's departure causes a terrible disturbance, but it does not leave the victim maimed or diminished. Christ commands both silence and release. Athanasius sees the silence as protection against receiving even true words from an impure teacher. The Lord therefore defeats evil on two fronts: he refuses its attempt to control the testimony about him, and he ends its control over the man, preserving the person while expelling the oppressor.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable and St Athanasius of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:31–37

verses.text: And fear came upon them all, and they spoke among themselves, saying, ‘What word is this? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they go out.’
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: The assembly recognizes that Christ's word accomplishes what it commands. Bede contrasts borrowed ministry with the Word himself, who acts in his own power.
verses.commentary: Theophylact reduces the assembly's wonder to its decisive point: Jesus says, “Go out,” and the spirit goes out. Nothing separates command from effect. Bede distinguishes this authority from the ministry of holy people. Saints may cast out spirits by the word of God, but Christ is the Word himself and performs mighty works by his own power. The fear that falls on the witnesses is therefore more than alarm at an extraordinary event. They are confronted with a speaker whose word rules the spiritual enemy directly. Their question opens toward faith: if the command carries such authority, then the identity of the one who speaks must be faced.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable and Theophylact of Ohrid, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:31–37

verses.text: And news of him spread into every place of the region.
verses.author: St Ambrose of Milan
verses.insight: The report spreads because mercy has become visible. The teaching heard in the synagogue is confirmed by a liberation the surrounding country can no longer keep private.
verses.commentary: The Catena treats the spreading report within the whole movement of teaching and healing at Capharnaum. Ambrose emphasizes that Jesus continues among an unbelieving people by alternating instruction with merciful works, seeking to soften their hearts. Cyril likewise says that mighty deeds awaken those not yet inclined toward knowledge. The news is therefore not mere celebrity. It carries the public trace of a word that has restored a suffering man. What began inside the synagogue moves outward through the region, giving others reason to seek the physician. Christ's fame follows his mercy because his authority has been exercised for deliverance, not display.
verses.source_label: St Ambrose of Milan and St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:31–37
